briefing: Toronto's October 26 mayoral vote is down to the wire, with one pollster calling Chow and Bradford neck-and-neck. Oil hovers near $110 on the Hormuz shutdown, keeping fuel and inflation pressure on Ontario households. Alberta's vote to stay in Canada is settled, and Bank of Canada and U.S. Fed rate decisions arrive October 28.
headline: Toronto mayoral race tightens as oil stays near $110

keyDates.label: B.C. provincial election
keyDates.why: British Columbians vote in Premier David Eby's snap election; advance voting runs October 16–21.

keyDates.label: Ontario municipal elections
keyDates.why: Toronto, Mississauga, Markham and every other Ontario city elect mayors, councillors and school trustees; Toronto polls open 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. The final televised mayoral debate is October 22.

keyDates.label: Israeli election; Queen's Park returns
keyDates.why: Israel votes amid talk of another strike on Iran, and Ontario's legislature sits again after a 21-week break.

keyDates.label: Bank of Canada and Fed decisions
keyDates.why: Both central banks set rates the same day; traders see about a 44% chance the Fed raises after hot U.S. inflation.

keyDates.label: U.S. midterm elections
keyDates.why: Control of Congress decides how much room Trump has on tariffs and the Iran war.

stories.backstory: The U.S. and Israel began striking Iran on February 28, 2026, in the middle of nuclear talks. The first wave killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei. Iran answered with missiles and drones on Israel, Gulf states and U.S. bases, and closed the Strait of Hormuz, the channel that roughly a fifth of the world's oil normally passes through. A peace memorandum signed in June briefly reopened shipping, but it fell apart in July when Iran started attacking commercial ships again to press its claim over the strait.
stories.headline: Brent holds near $110 as Hormuz tanker attacks continue
stories.impact: This is a big part of why gas and diesel in Ontario stay expensive: GTA regular is forecast around $1.80 a litre on Friday and diesel near $2.65. Diesel feeds straight into grocery and delivery prices, and higher fuel is one reason the Bank of Canada has been cautious about cutting rates.
stories.now: Brent touched $111.99 on Tuesday, the highest since May, before settling at $108.79 after unconfirmed reports that Qatar and Pakistan are working on a proposal to revive Iran talks. Early Wednesday it was back near $109.7 to $110.4, with U.S. crude (WTI) near $98.6. Iran's Revolutionary Guard said Tuesday that two 'non-compliant' tankers were struck in the strait, a claim not independently confirmed, and Kpler counts at least 18 vessels attacked in two weeks. Worries have spread beyond Hormuz to other shipping routes and crude-loading sites, including the Red Sea. Iran says its reopening plan, which depends on Washington lifting its blockade of Iranian ports and easing sanctions, still stands, but talks remain stalled.

stories.why: This is the single biggest driver of global energy prices this year. Sinkings are rare, so two in a day signal Iran is willing to raise the stakes for all cargo, not just oil tankers, which can push up shipping and insurance costs.

stories.backstory: Premier Danielle Smith announced the referendum in February and added the separation question in May. A yes on that question would not take Alberta out of Canada; it would start a process toward a later, binding referendum. Other questions ask about provincial control over immigration, proof of citizenship to vote, and making provincial law override federal law.
stories.headline: Alberta votes about 75% to stay in Canada in separation referendum
stories.impact: Indirect for Ontario, but a strong separatist showing would dominate federal politics and could affect transfer payments and national programs that every province shares.
stories.now: Unofficial results put 'remain' at roughly 75–77% and the separation-path option near 25%. In a televised address, Smith said she will honour the mandate and not hold another referendum on this issue while premier, adding that disputes will be settled through political and legal institutions and that many battles with Ottawa lie ahead. Carney said Albertans and all Canadians will move forward together with renewed purpose. Separatist leader Keith Wilson said the result shows at least a quarter of Albertans want Alberta treated better. The separation question was one of ten on the ballot, and final official counts were not yet confirmed at this refresh. Smith also vowed to use every legal and political tool to advance Alberta's interests and warned of a firm response if Ottawa interferes; Carney spoke with her Tuesday about closer cooperation, including on immigration.

stories.why: Even a non-binding result shapes national politics, federal-provincial relations and investor confidence in the energy sector.

stories.headline: Canada's inflation edges up to 3.1% as gas prices surge
stories.summary: Statistics Canada says consumer prices rose 3.1% in the year to September, up from 3.0% in August, led by gasoline up 27.8%. Core measures eased to about 1.9%.
stories.now: The annual rate was just under the 3.2% economists expected. Excluding gasoline, prices rose 2.2%, down from 2.4% in August. Fuel oil jumped 57.8%, hitting Atlantic Canada hardest, and shelter inflation rose to 1.8% from 1.5%. The Bank of Canada's preferred median and trim measures averaged 1.9%, down from 2.0%. Grocery inflation slowed to 1.7% from 2.8%.
stories.backstory: Oil prices jumped after the U.S.-Iran war closed much of the Strait of Hormuz earlier this year, and fuel costs have fed through to inflation since. Brent fell to about $74 in late June when shipping recovered, then climbed again as attacks resumed this autumn. Canada's central bank has weighed whether an energy-driven spike is temporary or will spread to other prices.

timeline.event: Brent near $114 as Hormuz violence flares
Oil falls to about $74 as shipping recovers
Inflation at 3.0%
U.S. inflation hits 3.7%
Canada's September inflation at 3.1%

stories.why: Core inflation easing while headline rises suggests the pressure is mostly fuel, which makes the Bank of Canada's October 28 decision a closer call. A hold looks easier to defend than a hike.
stories.impact: Expect high pump prices to keep squeezing GTA commuters and delivery-dependent costs. Since core prices are calm, mortgage holders may not face higher rates, though U.S. rate moves could still push borrowing costs.

stories.backstory: The Iran war, and especially attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, pushed oil above $100 a barrel this year. U.S. gas averaged about $2.98 a gallon before the war, and diesel hit a record $6.29 in late September. Wages are rising about 3% a year, slower than prices, so many Americans are falling behind. Rising long-term borrowing costs have also hit stock markets, especially debt-heavy AI companies.
stories.headline: U.S. inflation jumps to 3.7% as gas prices hit records
stories.impact: U.S. bond yields help set Canadian fixed mortgage rates, so GTA homeowners renewing soon could see higher offers. Fuel costs feed into everything from groceries to delivery prices in Ontario.
stories.now: The U.S. consumer price index (CPI) rose 0.6% in September and 3.7% from a year earlier, up from 3.4% in August and above the 3.6% economists expected. Gasoline jumped 9.1% in the month, and the U.S. average pump price hit a record $4.33 a gallon; core inflation, which leaves out food and energy, rose to 2.6%. CME Group data showed traders putting about a 44% chance on a quarter-point Fed hike on October 28, up from roughly 20% before the report. The 10-year U.S. Treasury yield touched 5.30% earlier this month, its highest since 2002, before easing to about 5.05% Thursday, and the average 30-year mortgage rate rose to 7.56%. White House adviser Kevin Hassett blamed the jump on Houthi attacks on Saudi oil sites.

stories.summary: American consumer prices rose 3.7% in the year to September, driven by fuel, and traders now see a real chance the Federal Reserve raises rates on October 28.

Ceasefire collapses after attacks on Hormuz shipping.
U.S. gas averages a record $4.33; diesel hits $6.29.

September CPI comes in at 3.7%.

stories.why: Higher U.S. inflation and interest rates ripple into Canada through borrowing costs, the dollar and trade. It also sharpens the cost-of-living debate three weeks before the midterms.

stories.backstory: The U.S. Supreme Court struck down Trump's broad emergency tariffs in February, but sector tariffs on steel, aluminum, autos, copper and lumber stayed. At the first CUSMA review on July 1, the U.S. refused to extend the deal for a full new term, so it now needs annual reviews. Ottawa walked out of talks on August 21, calling Washington's last-minute demands unfair. The U.S. imposed 50% tariffs on August 22, and Canada matched with counter-tariffs on September 8, plus a $25B support package for affected workers and businesses.
stories.headline: Trump says Canada will end up the 51st state; Ford says never
stories.impact: Tariffs raise prices on some U.S. goods in Canadian stores and squeeze manufacturing jobs in the GTA, Windsor and Hamilton. If you or your family work in autos, steel, logistics or anything that ships to the U.S., this is the story most likely to touch your paycheque.
stories.now: Speaking in Bullhead City, Arizona, on Wednesday, Trump said Canada will end up as the 51st state, argued the U.S. does not need Canada, and again floated renaming Lake Ontario. He pointed to Canada's dairy tariffs and to automakers moving plants to the U.S. Ontario Premier Doug Ford answered that Canada's sovereignty is not for sale. Earlier that day U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra suggested that Industry Minister Mélanie Joly's talk of aiming counter-tariffs at particular U.S. states could look like interference in the November 3 midterms, while Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre toured Michigan arguing for tariff-free auto trade. Separately, a draft joint statement seen by The Canadian Press shows Canada and the European Union planning closer ties on digital security, critical minerals and a proposed fleet of Canadian-built water bombers ahead of a summit at the end of October.

stories.why: About three-quarters of Canada's exports normally go to the U.S. Ontario, with its auto plants and steel mills, is the most exposed province.

stories.backstory: Russia's full-scale invasion is in its fifth year. U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have been trying to coax Moscow back to talks, and reportedly see letting Russian diesel back onto the market as a carrot. European intelligence services warn Russia may take bigger risks against NATO countries in the coming months.
stories.headline: Russia hits nine Ukrainian regions as EU leaders pledge support to Zelenskyy
stories.impact: Ukrainian hits on Russian refineries can tighten world diesel supply, which matters because diesel already feeds grocery and delivery costs in Ontario. Canada is a NATO member and a major Ukraine backer, so a widening split between Washington and Kyiv affects Ottawa's defence and aid decisions.
stories.now: The Associated Press reports Russian attacks hit nine regions overnight, damaging homes, wounding at least 15 people and forcing emergency power cuts for hundreds of thousands of households; grid operator Ukrenergo asked people to limit heavy appliance use in the evening peak. The UN human rights office says 328 civilians were killed and 2,105 wounded in September, 85% more than a year earlier. Russia claims it shot down 644 Ukrainian drones overnight, disrupting about 160 flights at Moscow airports. At the EU summit in Brussels, Zelenskyy thanked European leaders and said Ukraine must prepare for winter because Russia shows no sign of wanting peace; a day earlier he said he felt betrayed by Trump over cuts to intelligence sharing, limits on SpaceX's Starshield service and a U.S. deal on Russian diesel.

stories.summary: Overnight Russian strikes on nine regions caused emergency blackouts for hundreds of thousands of homes, while EU leaders meeting in Brussels promised to keep backing Ukraine and urged Washington to lean on Moscow. Ukraine has also vowed to keep hitting Russian refineries, which is feeding oil prices.

stories.why: Refinery strikes are Ukraine's main way to squeeze Russia's oil income, and dropping the pause puts Kyiv openly at odds with Trump's ceasefire push. With winter coming and Ukraine's grid badly damaged, the fight over energy targets could shape the next phase of the war.

stories.backstory: Chow won a 2023 by-election after John Tory resigned and is now seeking a full term. Bradford, a councillor, is her main challenger. Late-summer polls had Chow around 50% and Bradford near 39%. Big themes are housing costs, traffic, property taxes and the province's moves on bike lanes.
stories.headline: Chow and Bradford neck-and-neck days before Toronto votes
stories.impact: You get a vote for mayor, ward councillor and school trustee in your own city. Check your municipality's site for your polling station and advance-voting hours.
stories.now: Chow promised 15,000 new youth jobs, a guarantee that 20% of Scarborough East LRT construction jobs go to local residents, and $28 million for youth violence prevention, mentorship and employment programs. Bradford called her campaign out of steam, pledged to push the Eglinton East LRT in his first 100 days with construction starting by 2030, and repeated plans to remove 12 km of red bus lanes in Scarborough. The two also clashed over Bradford's proposed Toronto Water utility, which he says would stay fully public and Chow says could hand control to the province. Bradford also unveiled a $143 million plan to hire 1,000 more police officers, including a satellite Ontario Police College campus in Etobicoke. A record 225,550 Torontonians voted in advance polls; the final televised debate airs on CP24 on October 22 at 7 p.m., and election day is Monday, October 26, with polls open 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. Chris Alexander quit the race on October 6 without endorsing anyone, though his name stays on ballots; a Liaison Strategies poll since then has Chow at 51% to Bradford's 46%. A Mainstreet Research poll taken Oct. 6–7 had Chow at 40.8% and Bradford at 38.3% among all respondents (margin of error 3.1 points), and its president said the race is going down to the wire. Global News described the race as neck-and-neck this week, while a Pollara survey had Chow ahead 53% to 46% among decided voters. Bradford also pledged a TTC event-service plan tied to the Toronto Waterfront Marathon, which Chow's campaign answered by accusing him of cutting service.

stories.backstory: Republicans have controlled both the House and Senate since January 2025, which has let Trump pass his agenda with few checks. Midterms usually go against the president's party, and Trump's approval is lower than at the same point in his first term. All 435 House seats and 35 Senate seats are on the ballot. A Democratic House could launch investigations and block spending and trade legislation.
stories.headline: Poll finds voters want change as early turnout runs ahead of 2022
stories.impact: A change in Congress could shift the odds of tariff relief for Ontario's auto, steel and lumber industries. Ottawa's trade strategy is partly being timed around the outcome.
stories.now: An AP-NORC poll taken October 8–12 found about half of registered voters want Democrats in charge of the House or Senate, about 4 in 10 prefer Republicans and 15% are undecided; about a third approve of Trump's job performance and about 8 in 10 disapprove of his handling of living costs. Georgia logged more than 180,000 ballots on its first day of early voting, about 55,000 more than in 2022, and North Carolina opened in-person early voting Thursday, with Texas starting Monday. The Justice Department sued California officials to stop the counting of mail ballots from about 20,000 people it calls likely noncitizens; Secretary of State Shirley Weber says no evidence was provided and Attorney General Rob Bonta says the state will not comply. In Texas, Democrat James Talarico reported raising $64 million last quarter against Republican Ken Paxton's $18 million. Republicans hold the Senate 53–47.

stories.backstory: The seven career colleges with the highest OSAP use received $385 million in provincial grants in 2024-25. Questions about whether some students were enrolled in genuine programs have led to court challenges and earlier OSAP bans for a few colleges, extended this week by three years.
stories.headline: Ontario's OSAP freeze hits ballet, divinity and film students
stories.impact: If you or your child attends a private post-secondary school in Ontario, OSAP money may be delayed; contact the school's financial aid office and watch for the promised bridge loans.
stories.now: Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn paused Ontario Student Assistance Program (OSAP) payments to private institutions last week while accounting firm KPMG audits OSAP use at career colleges; preliminary findings were serious enough that he referred the matter to the Ontario Provincial Police. The freeze also covers private universities, chiropractic and naturopathic colleges, performing arts schools and theological schools. About half of the National Ballet School's teacher-training students rely on OSAP, and OSAP-funded tuition is about 10% of McMaster Divinity College's revenue. Quinn says he is working with banks on low-interest loans for affected students but has not given a timeline.

sources.title: CP24/Canadian Press: Students affected by OSAP pause
CP24: Ontario blocks career colleges from OSAP for three more years

stories.summary: Ontario's pause on student-aid payments to all private post-secondary schools, made during an audit of career colleges, is catching students at places like Canada's National Ballet School and McMaster Divinity College.

timeline.event: Top seven career colleges draw $385M in OSAP grants.
KPMG audit flags problems; matter referred to OPP.
Several career colleges barred from OSAP for three more years.
Students at ballet, divinity and film schools report impact.

stories.why: Thousands of Ontario students depend on OSAP, and a broad freeze shifts the cost of a fraud crackdown onto students at schools not under suspicion.

stories.headline: Trump drops press secretary Katie Zacharia after five days
stories.summary: The White House's newest press secretary was let go within a week of starting, and Trump publicly backed chief of staff Susie Wiles amid questions about her future.
stories.now: Katie Zacharia served about five days, making her the shortest-serving White House press secretary, after a widely criticized first news conference and questions about her credentials. Bloomberg reports Trump publicly backed chief of staff Susie Wiles and moved to quash talk about her job. Trump spent Saturday in Florida and Kentucky, where a political rally was scheduled. The turmoil lands just over two weeks before the November 3 midterms.
stories.backstory: The press secretary is the administration's main daily voice to reporters and the public. Zacharia was the latest person in the job in Trump's second term. Staff instability has drawn attention as Republicans defend slim congressional majorities and polls show voters wanting change.

timeline.event: Zacharia begins as press secretary.
First news conference draws criticism.

stories.why: Messaging discipline matters for a party facing a tough midterm, and turnover signals how settled the White House is heading into the final stretch.
stories.impact: Limited direct effect in Ontario, but White House communications are the main channel for tariff and trade announcements that affect Canadian exporters.

stories.backstory: Cleveland-Cliffs bought Stelco in 2024. Ottawa approved the deal under the Investment Canada Act on the condition that it keep union jobs and most non-union positions, more than 1,500 in total.
stories.headline: Cleveland-Cliffs CEO calls Ottawa's Stelco threats bullying
stories.impact: Steel layoffs ripple through suppliers and local businesses across the Golden Horseshoe. It also signals how hard Ottawa will push on other foreign-owned plants in Ontario.
stories.now: Cleveland-Cliffs CEO Lourenco Goncalves told BNN Bloomberg on Thursday that Industry Minister Mélanie Joly's threats amount to bullying and harassment, saying the company did not expect to be treated like a pariah less than two years after buying Stelco. He called the cuts a business decision to concentrate production, says he intends to rehire the workers once trade conditions improve, and denies breaking the commitments made under the Investment Canada Act. Joly says everything is on the table, including forced sale of assets or financial penalties. The steelworkers' local expects 300 to 350 layoffs in Hamilton itself, with more at Lake Erie Works in Nanticoke, and the Ontario NDP wants Premier Doug Ford to push for public ownership.

stories.summary: Stelco's U.S. owner says it is ready to fight in court as it presses on with up to 500 Hamilton layoffs, after Ottawa threatened penalties or a forced sale.

stories.why: It's a test of whether Canada can enforce promises foreign buyers make, and a sign of how the trade war is landing on Ontario steel towns.

stories.backstory: The Houthis, an Iran-aligned movement controlling much of northern Yemen, joined the Iran war in late March by firing at Israel. Since then the fight has widened into a direct Saudi-Houthi confrontation, with Houthi strikes on Saudi airports and on the East-West oil pipeline that Saudi Arabia uses to bypass Hormuz.
stories.headline: Houthi strike on Aden presidential palace kills five; Riyadh airport stays shut
stories.impact: Indirect but real: more disruption to Red Sea shipping means slower and pricier imported goods and another push on fuel prices in Canada.
stories.now: Yemen's health minister raised the toll from Thursday's attack on the al-Maashiq palace in Aden, seat of the Saudi-backed government, to five dead and 16 wounded; the prime minister and cabinet were unharmed. The Houthis say they targeted a Saudi military headquarters there, a claim Reuters could not verify. Saudi-led coalition spokesperson Turki al-Maliki says the Houthis have launched 20 attacks on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport this month, killing 17 people and wounding 333, plus attacks on Abha airport that killed three, and that coalition jets have destroyed 127 weapons depots and launch sites in Yemen. Riyadh's main airport is to stay closed until the evening of October 17, and more than 3,000 flights from Saudi airports were cancelled or grounded in a week. A Saudi official said the Houthis turned down a proposed meeting in Muscat, Oman, and Riyadh accused Iran of arming and training them. An EU–Gulf summit planned for October 24 in Riyadh has been postponed, and Trump says he is considering joining strikes on the Houthis. On Friday the Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted a ballistic missile aimed at the Red Sea port of Yanbu, two cruise missiles over the Red Sea and three drones over southern Saudi Arabia and the Riyadh area.

stories.summary: Yemen's government says a Houthi missile and drone attack on the presidential palace in Aden killed five people and wounded 16, the first strike on the complex in this conflict. Saudi Arabia says Houthi attacks on its airports have killed 20 people this month.

timeline.event: Houthi attack briefly shuts Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline.

stories.why: If the U.S. joins, the war gains another front, and the Red Sea route through Bab el-Mandeb could become as dangerous as Hormuz. That would hit the backup routes the world is relying on for oil and container shipping.

stories.backstory: Silver Rail is a kindergarten-to-Grade 5 school with about 459 students, in a city of roughly 100,000 in central Oregon. School shootings have become a recurring feature of U.S. life, and each one revives the debate over gun laws, school security and access to firearms by minors.
stories.headline: Teen gunman kills children at Oregon elementary school
stories.impact: No direct effect on Ontario, but U.S. shootings often prompt Canadian school boards and police to review lockdown procedures, and they feed into Canada's own debate over handgun and firearm rules.
stories.now: Police say the attacker forced his way through locked doors shortly before 1 p.m. local time Thursday and killed children aged 5, 8 and 11; a 7-year-old and a 54-year-old teacher were taken to hospital in critical condition. Early reports differed on whether the teacher died. Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said the 16-year-old was found dead minutes after the first call, and authorities say a bystander who pursued him into the school shot him. A law enforcement official told the AP the shotgun had been bought by his mother. All 32 schools in the Bend-La Pine district cancelled classes Friday, and the AP and USA Today database counts this as the 28th mass killing in the U.S. this year.

sources.title: CP24/AP: Teen shooter kills 4 at Oregon elementary school

stories.summary: A 16-year-old shot his way into Silver Rail Elementary in Bend, Oregon, on Thursday and killed three young children before a person who followed him inside shot him dead.

timeline.event: Gunman enters Silver Rail Elementary just before 1 p.m.
Attacker shot dead by a civilian who followed him.
All Bend-La Pine schools closed for the day.

stories.why: It is the 28th mass killing in the U.S. this year and lands weeks before the midterms, where gun policy is a live issue.

stories.backstory: Waymo runs paid driverless taxi service in several U.S. cities, including Phoenix, San Francisco and Los Angeles. Toronto would be its first Canadian market, and its winters and dense traffic are a tougher test than most of its current cities. Ontario's automated-vehicle pilot already allows Gatik's driverless box trucks to make deliveries for Loblaw in the GTA.
stories.headline: Waymo to start testing robotaxis on Toronto streets
stories.impact: Expect to see mapping cars with safety drivers on Toronto roads soon. Paid rides are still about two years away, but city council and the next mayor will face questions about curb space, safety rules and effects on taxi and Uber drivers.
stories.now: Waymo says the first phase, starting this year, will involve high-definition mapping of Toronto streets and test drives with a safety driver behind the wheel. The province approved the company under its pilot program for automated vehicles, and Toronto-based Element Fleet Management will handle maintenance and customer support. Waymo says its cars have logged more than 400 million fully driverless kilometres and were in 95% fewer serious-injury crashes than human drivers in its cities. Flavio Volpe of the Automotive Parts Manufacturers' Association called it a boost for Ontario's auto-tech cluster.

sources.title: CP24/Canadian Press: Waymo to launch robotaxis in Toronto

stories.summary: Alphabet-owned Waymo has Ontario's approval to begin mapping and testing self-driving cars in Toronto this year, aiming to carry its first paying passengers in 2028.

timeline.event: Gatik begins autonomous truck deliveries for Loblaw in Toronto.
Waymo announces Toronto testing under Ontario pilot.
Target for first Waymo passengers.

stories.why: It is the first big step toward driverless taxis in Canada and could reshape ride-hailing, taxi jobs and city transport planning.
